Hélène Hegaret et Caroline Fabioux : les microalgues toxiques et l'anoxie
Description:
Le deuxième épisode de notre Podcast est en ligne !! 🏄‍♀️ 
 
Dans cet épisode, nous sommes allées à la rencontre de Caroline Fabioux et Hélène Hegaret, un duo de chercheuses qui étudient les efflorescences de microalgues toxique au laboratoire de Laboratoire des sciences
de l'environnement marin (LEMAR) à Brest. Les toxines de ces organismes constitués d'une seule cellule et invisibles à l'œil nu, peuvent parfois se retrouver les poissons et les coquillages qui ont décidé d’en faire leur casse-croûte. Heureusement, de nombreux services de surveillance sont mis en place pour éviter que l’on se fasse empoisonner.  Au-delà de la consommation humaine, ces microalgues peuvent aussi avoir de gros impacts sur l'environnement en constante évolution avec le changement climatique. Dans cet épisode, nous explorons comment la recherche étudie ces petits organismes ainsi que les solutions qui existent pour le secteur de la pêche.

Titre: Catalyzing Marine Finfish Aquaculture Through Public Aquariums | AIE Webinar
Description:
Session Description
Public aquariums have unique opportunities to advance marine finfish aquaculture through their animal collections, technical expertise and capacity for research and innovation. Through the NOAA Sea Grant-funded project “Catalyzing Marine Finfish Aquaculture Through Public Aquariums,” a national network of public aquariums and academic institutions has worked to overcome persistent challenges in marine fish breeding and larval rearing.

This webinar will highlight the development of this collaborative network, technical advances achieved through shared expertise and the successful breeding and rearing of more than 20 marine fish species. We will discuss successes and challenges in broodstock management, egg collection, larval nutrition and juvenile production, as well as opportunities for technology transfer, workforce development and expanding marine aquaculture beyond public aquarium collections.

Breeding and Raising Fish for Aquariums StoryMap: https://arcg.is/1vuq0z3 

Speaker Bio
Dr. Andrew L. Rhyne is a professor of marine biology at Roger Williams University in Bristol, Rhode Island. His research focuses on marine aquaculture, larval culture, aquarium fisheries and the sustainability of the global aquarium trade. His work integrates applied aquaculture research with commercial production, public aquarium partnerships and conservation science. Through a longstanding partnership between Roger Williams University and the New England Aquarium, he has helped expand aquaculture research and production within public aquariums, including the recent completion of a NOAA Sea Grant-funded project focused on advancing marine finfish aquaculture through collaborative research and technology development.

Create your FREE AIE account: https://aquainfoexchange.org/register/  

This webinar was originally hosted on the Aquaculture Information Exchange (AIE). The AIE is a grant-funded project supported by NOAA and USDA. The Aquaculture Information Exchange website is hosted and maintained by Virginia Sea Grant.

Titre: Norway's AI Robots Use Lasers to Save Salmon! 🤖🐟
Description:
Norway is using thousands of AI-powered underwater robots equipped with precision lasers to protect farmed salmon from sea lice. Developed by Norwegian company Stingray Marine Solutions, the technology uses underwater cameras and artificial intelligence to detect parasites attached to fish. Once identified, a green laser targets and eliminates the lice without harming the salmon.

Sea lice are a major problem in fish farming because they can damage fish skin, cause infections, and even lead to death. Traditional treatments can also stress or injure the fish. Stingray's robots work 24/7 inside fish cages, detecting and removing parasites without taking the salmon out of the water. The system has reportedly helped protect more than 100 million salmon and trout, showing how AI and laser technology can make fish farming safer and more efficient.

But an innovative technology is changing the way this problem is handled.

Using underwater cameras and artificial intelligence (AI), this advanced system scans salmon and identifies tiny sea lice with remarkable precision. Once the parasites are detected, the system fires carefully targeted laser pulses to eliminate them.

The most fascinating part? The lasers are designed to target the parasites without harming the salmon.

This technology combines artificial intelligence, underwater cameras, and precision lasers to create a smarter approach to fish farming. It also shows how modern technology can help solve real-world challenges in aquaculture.

Norway is known for its salmon industry, and innovations like this demonstrate how science and engineering can transform the future of fish farming.

Titre: How Northern Norway Is Tackling Global Challenges With Innovation
Chaîne: Seriously Don't Do That With Dan Griffith
Description:
Could some of the solutions to global sustainability and technology challenges come from Northern Norway?

In this clip from Seriously Don't Do That™, Håkon Gustafson Giæver of Norinnova explains how the Arctic's traditional industries, natural resources, technical expertise, and research capabilities create opportunities for innovation.

Northern Norway's economy is closely connected to several important industries:

Fisheries and aquaculture.

Energy and minerals.

Tourism and space technology.

These sectors are often discussed through the challenges they face.

But Håkon asks viewers to consider their potential contribution to solving problems.

With the right combinations of research, technical expertise, and industry knowledge, established businesses can become important environments for developing and applying new solutions.

The discussion highlights the Arctic's role in connecting scientific research with real-world industry needs.

Rather than seeing traditional industries only as obstacles to sustainability, Håkon argues that they can help drive innovative responses to environmental, operational, and global challenges.

He also encourages viewers to look beyond geopolitical narratives about Northern Norway.

The region's importance is not limited to its borders or its strategic location.

It is also connected to the people, companies, and research institutions developing new technologies and approaches.

The Arctic should be viewed through the lens of innovation as well as geography.

For entrepreneurs, researchers, sustainability professionals, and investors interested in Arctic sustainability, aquaculture technology, energy innovation, marine technology, Nordic startups, and research commercialization, the region offers areas worth exploring.

Watch the full podcast with Dan Griffith and Håkon Giæver to understand more about Northern Norway's innovation ecosystem and its potential relevance to global markets.

Description:
Can fish-farm wastewater become a resource for sustainable aquaculture?

In this SAFE project video, our project partner, the Finnish Environment Institute (SYKE), demonstrates how process water from a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) can be used to cultivate microalgae for potential use in fish feeds.

By transforming nutrients from aquaculture process water into valuable microalgal biomass, SYKE is helping SAFE explore more circular and resource-efficient approaches to fish-feed production.

Titre: AquaBusiness #02 - Elane Correia (EC Consultoria)
Description:
🌊📊 AquaBusiness | O futuro da tilápia brasileira e as novas tendências do mercado

O mercado de pescado está mudando. Mas como a cadeia produtiva pode acompanhar as transformações no comportamento do consumidor e ampliar o consumo de pescado no Brasil?

No novo episódio do AquaBusiness, recebemos Elane Correia, Zootecnista, Consultora Técnica Comercial da EC Consultoria e Especialista em Pescado, para uma análise sobre a Seafood Show Latin America 2026, as tendências de mercado e os desafios e oportunidades para o futuro da tilápia brasileira.

🎯 Entre os principais pontos dessa discussão, três oportunidades merecem atenção:

🐟 1. Inovação e praticidade  
Novos produtos, porções adequadas, embalagens funcionais e informações claras sobre conservação e preparo podem tornar o pescado mais acessível e facilitar sua inclusão na alimentação cotidiana.

🇧🇷 2. Competitividade da tilápia brasileira  
Diante da concorrência dos produtos importados, é fundamental fortalecer o setor produtivo, destacar a qualidade do pescado nacional, valorizar a eficiência produtiva e ampliar a comunicação sobre a origem do produto.

📈 3. Agregação de valor e conexão com o consumidor  
Mais do que competir pelo preço, a cadeia do pescado precisa compreender as necessidades do consumidor e conectar produção, indústria e varejo para desenvolver soluções que estimulem o consumo.

💡 E qual será o futuro da tilápia brasileira?

A competitividade do setor dependerá cada vez mais da capacidade de inovar, entender o mercado e comunicar o valor do pescado produzido no Brasil.

O desafio não é apenas produzir mais, mas também agregar valor, conquistar o consumidor e ampliar o espaço do pescado na mesa dos brasileiros.

Titre: Inside the Feed Mill: Building the Future of Sustainable Aquaculture
Description:
This episode is sponsored by Undercurrent (https://www.undercurrentnews.com/) 


Episode Summary 


Aquaculture feed is far more than a mixture of ingredients. A modern feed mill brings together nutrition science, biology, technology, ingredient sourcing and manufacturing expertise to produce feed tailored to the needs of different species and life stages. Jose Luis Tejedor, CEO of the family-owned Tejedor Lázaro Group and DIBAQ Aquaculture, explains how that process works, from nutritionists developing species-specific formulations to the grinding, mixing, extrusion, drying, cooling and coating processes that transform raw materials into precisely sized pellets. The discussion also highlights why feed is such a significant consideration for farmers, affecting production costs, fish growth, health and feeding performance. 


The conversation also explores how aquaculture feed is evolving as the industry looks for more sustainable and efficient ways to produce nutrition for farmed fish. Feed manufacturers are increasingly exploring alternatives to traditional marine ingredients, including insect meal, bacterial proteins, plant-based proteins and algae, while also placing greater emphasis on responsible ingredient sourcing and deforestation-free supply chains. Advances in feed mill technology, sustainability certifications and nutrition research are helping manufacturers improve efficiency while addressing environmental challenges. Looking ahead, Tejedor sees opportunities in developing feeds for new species, supporting fish health in a changing climate and strengthening the role of feed manufacturers as technical partners to farmers. 


Featured Guests 

  •  Jose Luis Tejedor 
     CEO, Tejedor Lázaro Group and DIBAQ Aquaculture 

Key Topics Covered 

  •  The role of feed mills in modern aquaculture 
  •  How species-specific fish feed formulations are developed 
  •  The process of turning raw ingredients into finished aquaculture feed 
  •  Ingredient sourcing, quality control and traceability 
  •  The evolution of fish meal and fish oil use in aquaculture diets 
  •  Alternative feed ingredients, including insect meal, bacterial proteins, plant proteins and algae 
  •  Advances in extrusion and feed mill technology 
  •  Energy efficiency and more sustainable feed manufacturing 
  •  Sustainability certifications and responsible ingredient sourcing 
  •  Deforestation-free soy and environmental requirements for feed ingredients 
  •  The relationship between feed, fish health, farm performance and production costs 
  •  Future opportunities for aquaculture nutrition and new farmed species 

Key Takeaways 

  •  Fish feed is highly specialized. Feed formulations must account for differences between species, fish size, freshwater and marine environments, and specific nutritional requirements. 
  •  Ingredient quality is fundamental. Even advanced equipment and sophisticated formulations cannot compensate for poor-quality raw materials. 
  •  Aquaculture nutrition is moving beyond traditional marine ingredients. The industry is researching alternatives such as insect meal, bacterial proteins, plant proteins and algae to reduce reliance on fish meal and fish oil. 
  •  Feed mill technology continues to evolve. Manufacturers can improve production by optimizing existing equipment while also investing in machinery that reduces energy consumption and increases productivity. 
  •  Sustainability extends beyond the final feed formula. Responsible sourcing, traceability and considerations such as deforestation-free agricultural ingredients are increasingly important to feed manufacturers and their customers. 
  •  Feed influences more than growth. Nutrition can affect fish health, performance, feeding behavior and ultimately the economics of aquaculture production. 
  •  Feed manufacturers are becoming technical partners. DIBAQ's approach extends beyond selling feed to providing farmers with nutrition, health and production support. 
  •  The next generation of aquaculture nutrition will require continued innovation. New species, alternative ingredients, fish health challenges and environmental pressures will all shape future feed development.

Une équipe du Biodôme, dirigée par le Dre Nathalie R. Le François, et ses partenaires académiques, industriels et en biotechnologies examinent la possibilité d’utiliser une base de microalgues comme solution écoresponsable pour remplacer l’appât traditionnel.   

Dans cette vidéo, découvrez les premières expérimentations de pêche à l’oursin vert menées avec la Première Nation Wolastoqiyik Wahsipekuk au large de Cacouna.
